title: Discovering New and Emerging Markets
coreMove: Treat the first stage of market entry as learning under real conditions, not as a forecasting exercise that must be completed before contact begins.
sourcePressure: New and emerging markets are underdefined at the start: first users, use contexts, and demand patterns are not yet clear. Demanding forecast-level certainty before entering blocks the learning that real contact produces. Discovery is disciplined — not careless — but it operates by gathering evidence from real use rather than by modeling from a distance.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Reading this chapter as anti-planning or pro-experimentation-without-discipline, when the argument is for disciplined discovery — organized around what the team needs to learn, what boundaries to respect, and what evidence will count once contact begins.

hook: generic 'get out of the building' framing
counterintuition: generic 'just start talking to customers' counter
tryThisNow: generic 'talk to ten potential customers this week' prompt
examples: any scene that frames discovery as validation of a pre-existing hypothesis
any scene where the team simply 'interviews customers' without a specific learning question

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: Discovery episodes should feel like contact with something real — open in the moment of encounter, not in the planning meeting.

exampleSpecs.domain: medical device team learning from the first twelve patients to receive an early implant outside of clinical trial conditions
exampleSpecs.audience: a clinical product manager whose regulatory submission requires controlled trial data, but whose first commercial users are creating information the trial didn't capture
exampleSpecs.stakes: the commercial users are using the device in ways the clinical protocol did not anticipate, and that use is generating the most actionable information the team has seen
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Anna's weekly review of the first twelve commercial implants surfaces three use patterns the trial protocol never measured — not failures, but real-world applications that clarify what the device actually does for patients in normal care settings. The learning was not planned. It arrived because the team was in contact.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a clinical review board with twelve patient case folders open, three with handwritten notes in the margin
mustInclude: use patterns outside the trial protocol
the contrast between planned learning and arrived learning
mustAvoid: suggesting that clinical trials should be replaced by commercial observation

exampleSpecs.domain: language-learning app piloting with heritage speakers of minority languages rather than foreign-language learners
exampleSpecs.audience: a product manager whose market model was built around foreign-language learners in formal education settings
exampleSpecs.stakes: heritage speakers use the app differently than learners — they skip foundational lessons, seek vocabulary for family conversations, and want audio over text — patterns the product model didn't anticipate
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Chris's pilot with heritage speakers was not in the original market plan. The team ran it because a community center requested access. The usage patterns that emerged — which features got skipped, which got daily use — didn't match the learner model and revealed a real but unmapped market segment.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: an app session heatmap showing heritage speakers skipping the grammar module and spending three times longer in the audio vocabulary section
mustInclude: community center as the discovery entry point
mustAvoid: treating the heritage speaker segment as more culturally important than the learner segment

exampleSpecs.domain: electric bicycle fleet company testing urban office commuters in a city where the infrastructure was not designed for cycling
exampleSpecs.audience: a mobility startup director whose demand model was built on cities with existing bike lane infrastructure
exampleSpecs.stakes: the city has minimal bike infrastructure, which the model treated as a disqualifying condition — but real commuter use is producing different data
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Lukas has to decide whether to expand the pilot in the low-infrastructure city or wait for better conditions. The pilot data shows that commuters are finding routes the model hadn't mapped — shared sidewalk paths, parking garage shortcuts, and dedicated building access routes — and using them consistently.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a city map with official bike lanes in green and actual observed commuter routes added in pencil
mustInclude: observed routes not on the map
the decision to expand or wait
mustAvoid: implying that low-infrastructure cities are inherently unsuitable for cycling

exampleSpecs.domain: agricultural input company testing soil nutrient products with smallholder farmers in a new region
exampleSpecs.audience: a market development manager whose standard go-to-market model assumes farm sizes above 20 hectares and extension service infrastructure
exampleSpecs.stakes: smallholder farmers under 5 hectares are applying the product differently — smaller quantities, different timing, non-standard mixing — and the results are not what the usage protocol predicts
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Isabel predicts that non-protocol application will produce suboptimal results based on the standard trial data. The reveal shows that several smallholder adaptations — smaller dose timing matched to hand-application logistics — produce results comparable to the standard protocol on small plots. The discovery was not in any model.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a trial result table with smallholder rows flagged for non-protocol use and an unexpected result column
mustInclude: the comparable results in the reveal for adapted use
mustAvoid: implying that smallholder farmers are less sophisticated than large-farm operators

exampleSpecs.domain: modular housing company learning from disaster-relief deployments in ways that feed back into commercial product design
exampleSpecs.audience: a product director whose commercial market is urban workforce housing, not emergency response
exampleSpecs.stakes: the disaster-relief deployments were a grant-funded program, not a market entry — but the conditions they produced (rapid assembly, extreme weather, irregular terrain) have generated design insights not available in commercial deployments
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Anders's postmortem on the disaster-relief program wasn't supposed to inform commercial product design. The team conducted it as a compliance exercise. But the assembly challenges documented in the field — which subcontractors in disaster conditions could and could not do — revealed assumptions in the commercial design that no commercial deployment had yet stressed.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a post-hurricane deployment site with modular units being assembled by an unfamiliar subcontractor crew
mustInclude: grant-funded program as unintended discovery context
mustAvoid: treating disaster relief as a market to be commercialized

exampleSpecs.domain: cloud HR software team discovering that gig-economy platforms are using their scheduling module in an unanticipated way
exampleSpecs.audience: a product manager whose customer base is assumed to be traditional salaried employers managing W-2 employees
exampleSpecs.stakes: gig platforms are using the scheduling module for contractor assignment instead of employee scheduling — it works for their use case in ways the product team didn't design for and the support team wasn't trained for
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Before: Hiroshi's team treats gig platform usage as an edge case and routes their support tickets to a lower tier. After: the team interviews five gig platform operators, documents the specific scheduling logic they are using, and discovers that the module handles contractor assignment as well as it handles employee scheduling — a real market the product team had not modeled.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a support ticket queue with five gig platform tickets marked 'non-standard use — refer to advanced support'
mustInclude: the documented market in the after
mustAvoid: implying that traditional employer use cases are less important than gig-economy ones

skillTargets: distinguish forecast-first thinking from disciplined discovery in a described scenario
identify what a team needs to learn in an emerging market situation
recognize when an unplanned use pattern is a discovery opportunity rather than an anomaly
apply discovery-before-forecast reasoning to a non-technology emerging market
evaluate whether a described market entry approach is appropriate for the stage of market formation

tryThisNowSpec: Name one market your organization has decided it cannot enter yet because the forecast isn't clear enough. Write down one specific question — not a forecast, a question — that real contact with potential users would let you answer within the next month.

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that directly addresses the reader about what they are waiting to learn before they act — and asks whether contact would resolve it faster than modeling
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'
